trial_name: PROCOAG — Early 4F-PCC in Trauma at Risk of Massive Transfusion (2023)
citation: Bouzat P, Charbit J, Abback P-S, Huet-Garrigue D, Delhaye N, Leone M, et al; PROCOAG Study Group. Efficacy and safety of early administration of 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate in patients with trauma at risk of massive transfusion: the PROCOAG randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2023;329(16):1367-1375.
trial_type: RCT — multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled superiority trial
one_liner: Empirical early administration of 4F-PCC in trauma patients at risk of massive transfusion did not reduce 24-hour blood product consumption and significantly increased thromboembolic events.

pico.population: Adult trauma patients (>=18 years) requiring early RBC transfusion and judged at risk of massive transfusion (ABC score >=2 or clinician judgement)
pico.intervention: Early IV 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC; 25 IU factor IX/kg, 1 mL/kg at 120 mL/h) alongside protocolised trauma hemorrhage management
pico.comparison: Placebo (0.9% saline, 1 mL/kg) alongside protocolised trauma hemorrhage management
pico.outcome: Primary: total allogeneic blood products (RBC, FFP, platelets) within 24 hours; Safety: thromboembolic events within 28 days

background.existing_knowledge: Traumatic haemorrhage is a major driver of preventable early death. Trauma-induced coagulopathy is common and increases transfusion requirements and mortality. Standard component-based resuscitation is effective but can face delivery delays and may not rapidly correct factor depletion.
background.knowledge_gap: 4F-PCC rapidly restores vitamin K-dependent factors, but trauma use is off-label and largely supported by observational data. Whether empirical early 4F-PCC provides clinical haemostatic benefit on top of modern transfusion protocols without excess thrombotic harm was uncertain.
background.hypothesis: In severe trauma requiring early RBC transfusion and at risk of massive transfusion, early 4F-PCC (25 IU factor IX/kg) reduces 24-hour allogeneic blood product use compared with placebo without excess 28-day thromboembolic complications.

methods.design: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled superiority trial stratified by centre across 12 French level I trauma centres (Dec 2017 to Aug 2021).
methods.setting: 12 French level I trauma centres during early emergency department resuscitation.

inclusion: Adults (>=18 years) with severe trauma (grade A trauma team activation)
Requiring RBC transfusion prehospital or within 1st hour after admission
Considered at risk of massive transfusion (ABC score >=2 or clinician judgement)
exclusion: Traumatic cardiac arrest with ongoing CPR at admission
Known congenital coagulopathy or bleeding disorder

methods.intervention: 4F-PCC 1 mL/kg (25 IU factor IX/kg) IV via syringe pump at 120 mL/h as soon as possible after randomisation (median start 35 min post-admission) alongside protocolised trauma management including tranexamic acid and components.
methods.comparison: Placebo (0.9% saline) 1 mL/kg with identical appearance and delivery conditions alongside standard protocolised trauma hemorrhage management.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (patients, treating clinicians, investigators, outcome assessors, statisticians); masked drug prepared by unblinded nurse and hospital pharmacy.
methods.sample_size_power: 324 patients required to detect a 3-unit reduction in 24-hour blood product use (from mean 12 to 9 units; 25% relative reduction) with 80% power at two-sided alpha 0.05. Primary analysis used modified ITT.
methods.primary_outcome: Total allogeneic blood products (units of RBC, FFP, and platelets combined) consumed within 24 hours.
secondary_outcomes: Fresh frozen plasma units within 24 h
Time to PTr <1.5 among severe coagulopathy (minutes)
At least 1 thromboembolic event by day 28
methods.follow_up: Primary outcome tracked to 24 hours; clinical, mortality, and thromboembolic safety outcomes tracked to 28 days.

headline_bullets: Empirical 4F-PCC did not reduce 24-hour total blood product consumption (median 12 vs 11 units; P=0.72).
No differences were observed in component transfusions, time to haemostasis, or mortality at 24 hours or 28 days.
4F-PCC significantly increased 28-day thromboembolic events (35% vs 24%; RR 1.48; P=0.03).

outcomes_table.outcome: Total allogeneic blood products within 24 h (RBC+FFP+platelets)
outcomes_table.note: Primary end point; median (IQR); analysed n=164 vs n=160

outcomes_table.outcome: Time to PTr <1.5 among severe coagulopathy (minutes)

outcomes_table.note: Safety end point; passive surveillance; n=161 vs n=157 evaluable

safety: >=1 thromboembolic event by day 28 occurred in 56/161 (35%) in 4F-PCC group vs 37/157 (24%) in placebo group (RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.10, P=0.03).
Ancillary thrombin generation analysis demonstrated procoagulant shifts post-4F-PCC administration, supplying a potential mechanism for thrombotic harm.

domains.notes: Computer-generated variable block sizes (2/4/6), stratified by centre; central sequential sealed envelopes prepared by pharmacy ensured allocation concealment.
Double-blind design; primary end point (blood units) is objective; thromboembolic outcomes relied on passive surveillance, introducing potential detection variability.
327 randomised; 3 excluded due to consent withdrawal; modified ITT analyzed 324 (164 vs 160); per-protocol met in 308/324 (95%).
95% received study product within 1 hour (159/164 vs 149/160); median time to treatment was 35 (25–53) min vs 30 (21–47) min.

ISS 36 vs 36, SBP 89 vs 90 mmHg, lactate 5.4 vs 5.6 mmol/L, PTr >1.2 in 65% vs 68%; prehospital SBP higher with 4F-PCC (101 vs 90 mmHg). Co-interventions had minor imbalances: TXA 76% (124/164) vs 86% (138/160), fibrinogen 3g vs 3g, time to first FFP 73 vs 91 min.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate-to-strong for transfusion outcomes due to blinding and high protocol adherence, though safety evaluation is limited by passive surveillance and slight co-intervention imbalances.

domains.notes: Represents major adult trauma in high-resource level I trauma centers with rapid component therapy; excludes pregnancy, severe burns, and ongoing CPR.
Applicable to trauma systems delivering early component therapy and TXA; results may not apply to settings with delayed plasma access, factor-first resuscitation protocols, or low resources.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is moderate, offering clear applicability to high-resource trauma systems but uncertain generalisability to alternative resuscitation models.

strengths: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled methodology in an acute emergency setting.
Ultra-early administration (median 35 min from arrival) testing the peak window of trauma coagulopathy.
High protocol adherence (95% per-protocol) and objective primary endpoint.
Pragmatic trial execution across 12 level I trauma centres.
limitations: Empirical inclusion based on clinical risk rather than viscoelastic testing or laboratory-proven factor depletion.
Primary endpoint (component consumption) is operational/behavioral rather than direct clinical mortality.
Co-intervention imbalances, including lower tranexamic acid administration in the 4F-PCC group (76% vs 86%).
Thromboembolic event surveillance was passive rather than systematic, risking detection bias across centres.

critical_appraisal.summary: PROCOAG is a high-quality double-blind RCT demonstrating that empirical 4F-PCC does not decrease blood product use in major trauma and raises thromboembolic risk.
strengths: Rigorous double-blind placebo control in hyperacute resuscitation
Rapid median time to study drug delivery
High per-protocol adherence across 12 level I trauma units
weaknesses: Empirical enrollment without viscoelastic or factor-level targeting
Passive safety surveillance for thromboembolic events
Minor imbalances in baseline co-interventions (TXA treatment)

sections.authors_conclusion: In patients with major trauma at risk of massive transfusion, early administration of 4F-PCC did not reduce 24-hour blood product consumption and increased thromboembolic events.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Routine empirical early 4F-PCC should not be administered to unselected trauma patients at risk of massive transfusion.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult major trauma patients requiring early blood transfusion in settings with rapid access to component-based damage control resuscitation.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean PCC has no role in trauma; targeted therapy for known factor deficiency, specific viscoelastic profiles, or warfarin reversal remains indicated.
implementation_caveats: Empirical 4F-PCC increases 28-day thromboembolic risk (RR 1.48) without reducing transfusion requirements.
Shift resuscitation practice toward phenotype-guided haemostatic administration using viscoelastic assays or laboratory monitoring.
Maintain vigilant thromboembolic surveillance if PCC is administered.

controversies.notes: JAMA correspondence argued empirical inclusion of patients without proven factor deficits dilutes benefit and exposes non-coagulopathic patients to thrombotic risks.

controversies.topic: Laboratory PT correction vs functional haemostasis
controversies.notes: Commentary stressed 4F-PCC normalises prothrombin time but fails to correct fibrinogen or platelet deficits, offering negligible incremental gain when component protocols are established.
Ancillary thrombin generation analysis demonstrated procoagulant shifts post-4F-PCC, confirming a mechanistic foundation for the observed thrombotic harm.
Prior observational studies favoring PCC were highly susceptible to confounding and unstandardised safety tracking, as confirmed by systematic reviews.
The European trauma bleeding guidelines advise against empirical factor concentrate therapy, recommending targeted treatment guided by laboratory or viscoelastic testing.
The FiiRST-2 RCT (2025) similarly showed early fibrinogen concentrate plus PCC was not superior to plasma for 24-hour blood component use.

context_related_trials.relation: 2025 RCT finding early fibrinogen concentrate plus PCC was not superior to frozen plasma for 24-hour blood product consumption.

unresolved_questions: Does 4F-PCC offer net clinical benefit in a subgroup enriched by rapid point-of-care viscoelastic testing showing severe factor deficiency?
What is the optimal safety profile and dosing strategy of 4F-PCC when integrated into targeted resuscitation paradigms?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Empirical early 4F-PCC does not reduce blood product needs in major trauma and increases thromboembolic risk; adopt phenotype-guided resuscitation instead.
